utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome back to this courtroom. Today, we'll restart to hear the case. And before that, I would like to remind all the parties that this Trial Chamber rendered a decision on the 3rd of July on the independent counsel's motion for Mr. Vidoje Blagojevic to instruct the Registrar to appoint new lead and co-counsel. It seems the translation of the whole decision will take some time, I will summarise relevant parts of the decision, especially for the benefit of the accused, Mr. Blagojevic. After careful assessment of the facts presented, and a review of the jurisprudence of the Tribunal and the international human rights standards, the Trial Chamber arrives at the following conclusions: First, in assessing whether assigned counsel for accused should be withdrawn, it is for the person seeking the withdrawal to satisfy the Registrar that he should exercise his discretion in the interests of justice. The burden of proof is squarely on the person requesting the withdrawal of assigned counsel to demonstrate good cause. Accused should, therefore, take great care in working with the Registrar to select their counsel. Two, there's no absolute right for an indigent accused to choose his or her assigned counsel. It is a limited right. It is within the Registrar's discretion to override the wishes of the accused if relevant and a sufficient ground exists for holding that it is necessary in the interests of justice. Thirdly, there's no right to co-counsel. Co-counsel may be appointed in the interests of justice, and upon the request of lead counsel. While serving under the direction of lead counsel, co-counsel is bound to carry out his or her professional responsibilities in the best interests of the accused and in accordance with all obligations under the rules, directives, and the codes of the Tribunal. Fourth, one aspect of the right to a fair trial is the right to expeditious trial. Immediately before or at any time after the commencement of trial proceedings, only in the most exceptional motions for withdrawal of counsel will be entertained as such replacement of counsel will have an effect on the accused's right to be tried expeditiously. Fifth, in this case, the Trial Chamber recognises the friction exists between the accused and his counsel. Friction is not, however, equal to fundamental lack of trust due to misconduct or manifest inignitus [phoen]. Choosing to cease communications with counsel is not equivalent to counsel breaching his obligation to communicate and consult their client. Finally, Defence counsel have an ethical obligation to promote and build trust. Counsel should always act in the manner to earn the trust of their clients. The Trial Chamber called counsel to work with the legal representative assigned in accordance with this decision to rebuild the accused's trust in their professional abilities and their commitment to provide him with competent, diligent, and zealous representation in the proceedings before this Trial Chamber. Pursuant to Rule 54 and Rule 73 of the rules of procedure, the Trial Chamber dismisses the motion and orders that, first, the Registrar will appoint in consultation with the accused a legal representative to assist the accused and his Defence team in preparation of his Defence in accordance with terms specified below no later than ten days after the rendering of this decision. The legal representative must share counsel's objectives in assuring that the accused receives a fair and expeditious trial and a competent, effective, and a zealous Defence. Towards that end, the legal representative shall work with the accused and counsel, not simply as a bridge or interlocutor, but as a temporary addition to the accused's Defence team. And thirdly, the terms of the assignment of the legal representative are: The legal representative shall be a person who meets the qualification of counsel pursuant to Rule 44 and Rule 45 of the rules, and is currently on the list of counsel maintained by the Registrar pursuant to Rule 45 of the rules. The legal representative shall be assigned for a period of up to three months. The legal representative is a complement to the Defence team and is not a replacement. The accused must work with his counsel through whatever means they find the most appropriate while recognising that the legal representative's appointment is a temporary and extraordinary measure to normalise the situation. The legal representative has the right to appear in Court. The legal representative is bound by lawyer/client privilege. In the event that a accused has a specific issue he would like to raise before the Trial Chamber, he may do so through counsel or upon being granted leave through the legal representative. The legal representative will not have the right to examine and cross-examine witnesses. The decision is being translated in an expeditious manner, and we are told that the accused will get copy in B/C/S by this Wednesday. The Trial Chamber would like to inform the accused that you could seek certification for leave to appeal this decision if you are not satisfied with it. We have been informed that the independent counsel will be meeting you on the 14th of July to discuss the decision and any follow-up steps you may choose to make. The Trial Chamber will extend the period of time for you to seek certification until after you have a chance to read the decision and discuss it with the independent counsel. At the same time, the Trial Chamber will encourage you to work with the Registrar to select the legal representative and encourage you to rebuild your relationship with Mr. Karnavas and Mrs. Tomanovic as they are your counsel. In light of recent disclosure of new exhibits and the witness statement of Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Obrenovic, as well as the issue related to Mr. Blagojevic's counsel, the Trial Chamber will recommend to the Prosecution that it not call Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Obrenovic until after the summer recess. Thank you. Any observations? Yes, Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have understood what you have said now, and I think that I have followed as much as I could because, of course, for me, this is more or less new material. Your Honours, you must understand the situation. When a person is falsely accusing you of criminal and corruption, and you do not have a right or a possibility to resist that, furthermore, that person is then imposing themselves on you to defend you in such an important case. That's all I have to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Blagojevic, I could not agree with you in this aspect. Anyway, the reasons is very clear in that decision. We only hope that you could have the opportunity to discuss this matter with the independent counsel assigned by this Trial Chamber. As I said, if you are not satisfied with the decision, still you have remedies to make it up. You could file application for certification of appeal of this decision, and we will extend the time limits for you. Well, having said that, could we hear the witness. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we do have a witness, though we also have a new lawyer from the Prosecution which, if I could introduce, Antoinette Issa is a brand new lawyer with the Office of the Prosecutor, and also Ann Davis is with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Welcome to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we will take your recommendation and call Mr. Obrenovic and Mr. Nikolic after the break. And just so the record is clear, the charges mentioned by Mr. Blagojevic are nothing to do with charges brought by the Prosecution. We have our own different charges. It may be unclear from the way he stated that on the record. But we have Mr. Nesib Mandzic available, and we would call him at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I couldn't remember how to push the button on here. Your Honours, I do have one matter I would like to file with the Court a document. If you recall, in May we had a problem with an executive decision ordered by George W. Bush that created a felony for anybody to offer assistance or services to anybody on annex B, and Mr. Jokic's name still exists on annex B. I wrote to the Department of the Treasury, and my response from the Department of the Treasury is unacceptable and still does not relieve me from the threat of Prosecution by my government. I will make sure that the President of the Tribunal receives a copy of this today. But just for the record, I would like the Court to know that I have not been exonerated at this point under this executive order issued by George W. Bush. I would like -- I gave a copy to the Prosecutor but I'd like the Court to have a copy of this document and it to be filed as record in our trial also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will be very glad to receive that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I might have the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you could do that during the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Also, Your Honours, I forgot to introduce, we have Chris Murphy with us today. She is our case manager, and I want to welcome her to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Welcome to this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Examined by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, could you state your full name and spell your last name for us, please.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Nesib Mandzic, born in 1962 in Skelani Municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I am an electrical engineer. I have been working at the electrical company of Bosnia-Herzegovina with its seat in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you currently undergoing studies?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went to do postgraduate studies in electrical engineering. I finished all my exams, and I'm currently doing a dissertation. I'm writing up an MSC and I hope that in a few months I will complete it. Apart from these activities I am a member of the municipal assembly of Srebrenica, that is, of the municipal council and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you living in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: In the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long had you been living there?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I was born in Skelani in Srebrenica Municipality, but in the urban area of Srebrenica. And the enclave was part of that. I worked there from 1990 until July 1995. Also including the part of the war from 1991 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your occupation in July 1995? What kind of work were you doing?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I was a director of the secondary school, and I was lecturing at the same school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period, that summer of 1995, did you come in contact with any Dutch officers that would come by the school?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the course of 1994 and the first half of 1995, I had contacts with officers of the Dutch battalion and soldiers to our school, a Dutch officer came. I believe his name was Boering. He came and assisted us with acquiring some school material in difficult circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you on 11 July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: In the night between the 10th and the 11th of July, 1995, together with my colleagues, it was such a dramatic situation that occurred. We happened to be at the school. We spent the night there. We didn't sleep there, but just spent the night in such fear thinking and discussing where to go, whether to go through the forest, through the wood, or whether to go to the UNPROFOR base in Potocari. So on the 11th of July, we found ourselves in the secondary school, and it was about 1300 hours. Because of the attack of the Bosnian Serb army, we had to withdraw. Some of us went through the wood towards Tuzla and the others went to Potocari and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the day on 11 July, can you describe the situation that was happening around you and what you decided to do?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: The situation was a dramatic one. Every person and every face you can see that there was a fear of death because of the approaching of the Serb army because of their operations that were mostly going toward civilian targets. There were shells that were landing around the town, on the streets. There were people shouting, screaming for help, women with children. I saw helpless old people in the streets. Nobody could help them. Nobody could evacuate them. In such a situation, there wasn't a person either from the military or the political leadership, from the Bosnian authorities, to say you can go to the Potocari, to the DutchBat base or show us any other way out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you decide to do on the afternoon of the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Considering that I was wounded in 1993, and I was recovering from that, and it was at the end of May, beginning of June the field hospital of the DutchBat, there was surgery that was performed on me. I was not able to go through the wood. So I decided to go to the Potocari UN camp of the DutchBat, hoping that in that camp, like thousands of others, I would get protection considering that it was a demilitarised zone which would also include protection of civilian population. And it was on this basis that in the afternoon of the 11th of July, I arrived in Potocari in 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a demilitarised zone. In reality, was the enclave fully demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Mostly it was, if we look at the handover of the heavy weaponry of AA weaponry, of anti-tank weapons and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a Bosnian Muslim organisation though to a -- an army inside the enclave at that time in July? You said mostly.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: As far as I know about the organisation of real military formations, we can say that these were present in the Srebrenica enclave. There were certain symbolic units that were mostly -- they kept certain trophy weapons. They were close by to the area. What I mean to say is that these were people who had kept these trophy weapons. They lived in the areas where it was really necessary to keep some kind of security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us you decided to go to Potocari. Can you describe your -- how you went to Potocari and what occurred along the way?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: On the way to Potocari, the army of Republika Srpska was shelling the convoy, both on left and right side of the road creating a psychological pressure on the convoy to go and move towards Potocari without thinking about any other options.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe how many people were with you and describe this what you call a convoy of people as they move along the road towards Potocari.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: It was a convoy which was about 5 kilometres long. There were tens of thousands of people who were moving in the direction of Potocari. Mostly women, elderly people, people who were helpless. There was a lot of fear, panic, screaming in the course of that journey. Every single time a shell landed, there would be a mother throwing herself on the asphalt, with children crying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this large group of people mostly on foot or in vehicles?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Mostly, over 95 per cent, went on foot. There was a small group as much as I was able to see, people who could really hardly move, sick or elderly they were on lorries. And I noticed, I think, that there were people sick that were loaded from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any shells land in the crowd that was moving towards Potocari?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw shells landing before all those people set out for Potocari. Near the konfekcija building in Srebrenica, a shell fell on a group of people, several thousands of people. Later I heard that the shell had killed and wounded some of those people. On the way to Potocari, however, shells were falling left and right. I couldn't see clearly at that time, that any of the people travelling with me were injured. But people were saying that the convoys behind us suffered casualties, there were people who had been killed and wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About what time did you get to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Between 4.00 and 5.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: As most other people, I tried to approach the DutchBat camp in Potocari. We were not, however, allowed to do so. And then we returned to the same place as before, across the road. And we looked for a small shelter, sort of a refuge, to rest in the deadly heat and take shelter from Serb soldiers' gunfire nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That afternoon and early evening, can you briefly describe the situation in Potocari, how many people, what was going on?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: On the afternoon of the 11th of July in Potocari, there were about 30.000 refugees from the areas of a number of different municipalities. Most people were from Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica municipalities, Visegrad, Zvornik, and so on and so forth. At any rate, every single person was obviously in fear, afraid, even the smallest child. There was fear on the way from Srebrenica to Potocari. As on the previous days, the army of Republika Srpska was carrying out offensive operations aiming at cleaning the enclave of its Muslim population. The same afternoon, the shooting and shelling continued overhead, the aim of the shelling was intimidation of civilians to prevent them from even pondering their return, to make them accept the fact of deportation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there Dutch soldiers among the Muslim refugees in Potocari at that time?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the Dutch soldiers were in the camp in July 1995. They took refuge there alongside with about 5.000 refugees, but more than 20.000 refugees remained outside the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That evening, were you contacted by anyone from the Dutch battalion?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, they used a megaphone, and they called out my name. I didn't know what was happening, but when they called out my name, I responded, I was approached by an interpreter and an officer of DutchBat. They asked me to enter the camp because the commander of the Dutch battalion wanted to speak to me. They said the situation was very difficult and uncertain, both for the refugees and for the Dutch soldiers. I heard then that certain Dutch soldiers had been imprisoned, taken prisoner by the army of Republika Srpska, that Serbs were asking for negotiations to release them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you go to the Dutch camp and meet with the Dutch commander?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: As I said, they told me that the situation was difficult, that some Dutch soldiers had been captured, that under such difficult circumstances, there was nearly nothing they could do, that it was the Serbs setting the terms for these negotiations, and that the Serbs asked for a Bosnian delegation to also attend these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mentioned negotiations. Do you recall the name of the commander of the Dutch battalion that was speaking to you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say to you regarding your involvement in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans tried to convince me to go to these negotiations with the Serb side. He said he would support me in my intention, to ask for safe evacuation of refugees during those negotiations, for the refugees to be protected during the evacuation itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you say to him?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I told him that I was not representative of the civilian authorities and that it was difficult to understand under such unfair circumstances for me to appear on behalf of the civilian authorities. As far as I knew, the civilian authorities had fled through the woods. I had no authority, nor did I feel that I had any ability or capacity, to represent these civilian bodies of authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So today, you hold an office, but back then you were -- you didn't hold any kind of political office or in any sort of representation capacity. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans and his deputy major, Franken, convinced me and told me, yes, we know all that, but you're an intellectual, you're a man of the people. You're someone people trust and you can help in this difficult time. On the other hand, you have the Serb side insisting on these negotiations, there must be negotiations because the Serb side are requesting negotiations. And negotiations can be of assistance both to you, the refugees, and to the Dutch soldiers facing a very difficult situation. I was sweating from pressure. I was buckling under pressure. I was afraid of going to Bratunac. We had heard what had happened there in July 1992 when Bosniaks had been killed at the stadium. I was afraid of the situation as it was in Potocari. I was afraid to travel. I was afraid of the pressure I would be facing once I got there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: They took some time convincing me, the colonel of the DutchBat and his deputy, and I agreed to get in the car with them and drive to Bratunac to these so-called negotiations, although it was quite clear to me at the time that those were not too equally strong sides negotiating. I knew that these negotiations were a basic precondition for the survival of the population there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where in Bratunac did you go with DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: The Fontana Hotel, and the same night, the 11th of July, we arrived about 11.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, yesterday did you have a chance in my office to view some video of the meetings that occurred, that you were involved in both on the night of the 11th and the morning of the 12th?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you just a brief segment of that video that he is involved in in order to save some times, Your Honours. We don't, I don't think, need to see the entire segment. But before we get to that, I'd like to show you a few still photographs of some of the people that were at that meeting. And this should be Exhibit P27. Do you recognise that individual on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Apparently, we aren't -- his screen is the one that's not working --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see a clearer image now, but it's not all that clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we'll try it the old-fashioned way.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: This is the communications officer of the DutchBat in Srebrenica. This was the person I was talking about. He would see me at the secondary school, Major Boering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to the next photograph. This is Exhibit 28. Do you recognise that person?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the commander of the Dutch battalion, Mr. Karremans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were both Boering and Karremans at the meeting on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you could look at Exhibit P29, the next one, was this person at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was Petar, the interpreter. He works for the UN now in the Zvornik area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim interpreter or a Serb interpreter that night? Do you know who he was working for?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: He is a Serb himself. During the war, he worked as a UN interpreter. His job was with the UN, but he was interpreting for the Serb side. He's currently working as an interpreter for the UN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the next one, Exhibit P30. Was this person at the meeting that night of the 11th?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is an officer of the army of Republika Srpska. I saw him at the meetings at the Fontana Hotel in Bratunac. But I also saw him in Potocari. He used to come there to see how the deportations were going and whether everything was unfolding according to the plan of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know his name at the time?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't, although General Mladic did introduce them to us, all of them, the military and civilian representatives. But I did not remember his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next exhibit, 31.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: This is General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he at the meeting that night?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember where he was seated?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Next to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to P32.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now I will show you a brief segment from that evening and just ask you to watch it along with us and I'll ask you a question or two about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, how were you feeling at this point with General Mladic in front of you and you're speaking?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I was completely scared. I knew what had been happening between 1992 and 1995 in the Srebrenica enclave and outside the Srebrenica enclave in the neighbouring municipalities and across Bosnia-Herzegovina were persecutions of the Bosniak population, they were being driven out from Serb-held territory, the territory held by the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, let me just interrupt. Try to answer my question. I will ask you questions about those things, but we need to go question by question. You do mention that there are people in the enclave from many outlying municipalities. Can you just briefly explain how people from outlying municipalities ended up in the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: In early April, or rather May 1992, they had been driven from their homes and land by units of the Republika Srpska. And they found refuge in the villages around Srebrenica and in the town itself, in early May 1992. Those were refugees from other municipalities such as Zvornik, Bratunac, Vlasenica. Hundreds of people, of those refugees were killed and massacred by the army of Republika Srpska and paramilitary units coming from Serbian Sinagora [phoen] as they were trying to reach safety back in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could continue the tape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, how did you feel when General Mladic told you that people would survive, stay, or vanish, and talked about discussing the salvation of the Muslim people and stated that the future of your people was in your hands? How did those statements make you feel?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I was intimidated. General Mladic was talking about the disappearance of the Muslim people from the enclave, or outside the enclave for that matter. He said the destiny of your people in this enclave and even outside the enclave is in your hands. That's what he was saying. We knew that Gorazde, Brcko and the other enclaves were next. I felt great fear above all. I was thinking feverishly how I could help those people. I knew that death was awaiting them. This soldier, this general, this man, had his mind set on making a whole people disappear. The next day, at the next meeting, when --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hold on before we get there. We will get there. Let me ask you some questions. At the meeting on the 11th, was there material -- did things happen that were not on the video that you have been able to see, the complete video?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were a lot of symbols there, a swine being slaughtered in the neighbourhood near Fontana Hotel. It was supposed to be some kind of metaphor, you see this swine being slaughtered, it's exactly what we will do with you. There were other menacing messages by General Mladic. You see what your own political representatives did to you, Izetbegovic can't help you now, Ganic can't help you now. The only person who can help you now is Mladic himself, that's me. He was threatening us. And then at last he would say: "I'll show mercy. I'll let everyone go."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll show you another Exhibit P33. It should be right there since the machine's not working.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: This is the board of the Municipal Assembly of Srebrenica. When we first met in Bratunac, General Mladic put this board before me. He said put this in front of Nesib so he can have a look to see what it looks like. Or rather plaque. I saw immediately that the right-hand portion of this plaque, there was a piece missing where it said "Bosnia-Herzegovina" and there was a message across the board "This is the end of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the end of the old forms of living together in Bosnia and Herzegovina" or in Srebrenica municipality for that matter as it had been for centuries up until July 1992. When I say the different forms of living, I mean religious and ethnic tolerance and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. When the meeting -- thank you. When the meeting ended, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: When the meeting ended, I got on to the DutchBat vehicle and we headed back towards Potocari. That same night, I tried to reason, I tried to think how can we survive? And I had to think on behalf of all those refugees, how to draw up a list, how to answer Mladic's requests. I was at the camp, DutchBat camp, that night. I was trying to sleep, but I couldn't sleep. I had dark premonitions and a very dim view of what would happen to the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to a meeting the next morning at the Hotel Fontana as planned at 10.00?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. And we also expanded this Bosniak delegation. There was a Mrs. Camila Osmanovic and Mr. Ibro Nuhanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Ibro's last name?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Nuhanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nuhanovic with an N or with an M? Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: With an N.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. About what time did you arrive at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: About 10.00 a.m. in the morning on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now was General Krstic and General Mladic at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: And a number of other officers and members of the political leadership of the Bratunac Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name any of those political leaders from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I recall Miroslav Deronjic. I went to school with him. I also remember General Mladic also introduced members of the legislative authority of the Bratunac municipality, Mr. Simic. And I can't recall another man -- there was another man, but I can't recall him. He was from the political leadership of the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Colonel Karremans and Major Boering also at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, we came with them in the same vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll play another short segment of that meeting, if we could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, was the -- that's obviously just a short clip of that meeting. But was the substance of that meeting on the 12th any different, did it have any significant differences than the meeting that happened the night before?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: More or less General Mladic repeated the words, that he would ensure all the Bosniak population to leave and even to return to their homes but there were moments of psychological pressure like at this other meeting, one of his soldiers or officers would barge in during the meeting and they would say: "General, the Muslims have come to Bratunac unauthorised." And then at that moment, colleague Camila Osmanovic stood up and was that an association to 1992 of the killing of Bosniaks in Bratunac? I'm saying this was one of our impressions, impressions that we had. Also what was not defined and where General Mladic didn't give a straight answer to, like I asked him the first night at the meeting, is it going to be a safe evacuation of the population from the enclave, and it was mostly discussed at the level of the Red Cross and the coordination of UNPROFOR with an evacuation, safe evacuation, with dignity of the civilian population. Certainly there was pressure and the attack of the Serb soldiers, and such aspects -- this was disallowed to be discussed further by General Mladic. He stopped all that discussion. He didn't want that to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any mention of the Serbs wanting to see the military-aged men that were in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was one aspect in which pressure was applied. In Potocari, there was mostly elderly, women, children. That was true, people who had nothing to do with the war, war operations. They just happened to find themselves in such difficult circumstances in the war-torn zone. They just wanted to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you recall about the military-aged men being mentioned at that meeting, if anything?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: There was -- it was mentioned that certain Bosniaks who were younger, that there were some indications that some of them may have committed some offences and that they should be interviewed by the Officers of the Bosnian Serb army, and the DutchBat officers could be present at these interviews. And we reacted immediately. We said in Potocari, there are very few people who are in any connection with offences and crimes and murders. These are people mostly in Potocari who have spent the war in the enclave. They were there, they just happened to be there. They were not prepared for the war. They couldn't wait for the war to be over and they were mostly civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go after the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Well, with the vehicle of the DutchBat, we returned to Potocari, to the UN base. And together with the colleague Ibro Nuhanovic, we resumed our conversation how in which way we can make a list primarily of the male population because we could see that everything was revolving around the male population, that male population would be under threat, would be in danger, from 15 onwards, 15 years of age onwards. At that moment, myself and colleague Nuhanovic, who is no longer alive as of the 13th of July, 1995, we were speaking. We tried to make a table, an overview, which would be a good thing to have the data on the male population. And we heard from some distance, 150, 200 metres, we heard some noise, clamour, and we then suddenly realised the Serbian army had arrived, they had mixed in themselves with the civilians. So the very moment that that idea that we had listing and making a table of all the male population of 15 years of age onwards it was impossible to enforce, because already, 12th of July, after 1200 hours, Serb soldiers, Serbian army barged into the mass of people and it was impossible for us to do anything whatsoever, to see how many men were present in the place, in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to make a list of men inside the actual DutchBat camp?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, we tried to make a list, and we made a list, although I have to mention the great number of people, of adults, inside the base, inside the Dutch UN base, did not adhere to our idea of being on the list. They specifically asked me what if the Serb army get hold of that list? Are we going to be the first ones to be killed off? And I really couldn't explain to them how difficult this was. So finally people who had a lot of confidence in me and colleague Nuhanovic and others who were working on this list, we tried within a very short time, we wrote down the names of 239 people, mostly out of these people listed, 239 people, more than 90 per cent went missing. That is, the Serb army executed them. Time has passed since then, and knowing some of them, I have to say these people were civilians. They worked in factories before the war. They worked in the fields before the war. They tried to feed their families before the war, to make up for the lack of water and food in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work with DutchBat in preparing this list for the men that were actually inside the UN Compound as opposed to the people outside the compound?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we did. Yes. And in those preparations, because some of the persons did not want to be on the list, I went back to the base, that is, to the deputy commander of the DutchBat, Major Franken, and I said to him certain people do not want to be on the list. They are worried about the list falling into Serb hands? What do you think? Who should we give these details to? And he said, well, you can give me the list, and if the Trial Chamber will excuse me, he said he would put the list in his undergarments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so did you give him the list of 239?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did give a list of 239 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, did you see a photocopy of that list in my office?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the copy -- I saw the copy in October, sometime in October when journalists arrived in Tuzla. So it was not the first time for me to see this list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: October 1995 was the first time you saw it after the events?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Major Franken will be testifying, and that list will be an exhibit in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us what happened to Ibro Nuhanovic, the other person who was at the meeting with you representing the meetings?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. This person's name is Ibro Nuhanovic. He was a member of the so-called Bosniak negotiation team, negotiating group. And together with me, he worked on this list. And on the 13th of July, members of his family, that is his wife and his younger son, had to leave the DutchBat camp at the demand of the Serb army like the other refugees, and he knew that his wife and his son would be divided. And he couldn't, as a parent, as a spouse, he couldn't stand that. And Hasan, who was an interpreter at the DutchBat, he wanted Major Franken, he asked him to let his parents stay so they wouldn't have to leave with this group because he could see that there was a -- people being divided, males being separated from women and children. And Major Franken just shrugged and said, Hasan, I can't help you. Your brother and your mother have to leave, and your father can stay. But Mr. Nuhanovic couldn't stand that, separating from his family, from his spouse and his son. He left with them, and he left then and he was never seen again. He was killed and his wife as well, and his younger son, and the only person left from that family is his other son who is now in a very difficult psychological condition because of the loss of his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, do you think it might be a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, we now have you back at the DutchBat base after the meeting at the Hotel Fontana. About what time did you get back to the DutchBat base in Potocari on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Approximately before 1200 hours, so just before noon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you've described that the Serb army came in to the area outside of the DutchBat base. Were you able to actually see the people being loaded on buses and transported out of the area from where you were at the DutchBat base?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I didn't notice we didn't have Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Please accept our apologies. Excuse us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was able to see the arrival of the Serb soldiers in front of the UN base in Potocari. I was able to see they were distributing, in inverted commas, sweets and chocolate to the children. After about an hour, I was able to see from the window of the place where we were standing at the base, I was able to see the separation process, that is, the loading of women only on to buses which made me conclude that it was in that area that men were separated from women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you actually see men being separated or did you just see women only being put on buses?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: We saw a group, they were in front of the bus at a distance about 30 to 50 metres. So there were groups, mixed groups of refugees, men, women, elderly, men, women, children, adults, et cetera. Some 50 metres away from that group, there were parked buses and lorries. On the first day of the deportation, on the 12th of July, those buses in the hours of the afternoon, women were forcibly loaded on to buses while men were not loaded on to buses on that side where we were standing. The men were not deported. So this made us conclude that men were being separated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how long did you watch this process going on, on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I was able to see that throughout the afternoon, for hours, from about 1300 hours until well over 2000 hours. It was a horrific situation, very painful to watch. My colleagues were able to see it as well. All the people that were at the UN base, officers, soldiers of the DutchBat, including the refugees who were inside the base. Everybody was able to see this separation which then brought fear of death into the hearts of everyone who was inside and outside of the camp, over 20.000 people, and about 5.000 who were inside the camp, inside the base. I asked Major Franken to stop the evacuation because this evacuation, or rather deportation would bring to the execution of thousands of men. And we were also worried about the fate of young women, young girls, that they would be raped. Later on, after the arrival in Tuzla, we recognised the tragic situation, that some of my friends, fellow citizens from the same town, were raped. Because of religion and because of shame that they shouldn't be speaking about this, these raped young women, these young girls, did not turn to organs of authority or to the medical teams in order to say -- tell their story and say what happened, and they didn't ask for protection. This was something that was done within their families. These stories did not go outside their families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you asked to do anything that afternoon by any of the authorities?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I don't know which authority do you mean there? There was only the authority of the army of Republika Srpska and the power of the army of Republika Srpska. On the other side, there was just the presence of the Dutch soldiers and officers, and we were completely helpless. We were at the mercy of the officers and soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska and their superiors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to people outside the base that day?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe how that occurred.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Well, in the afternoon, about 1600 hours on the 12th of July, the interpreter and one of the surgeons of the DutchBat in Srebrenica approached me and my colleague, Nuhanovic, that I spoke about and about his tragic situation, that General Mladic wanted to see us, that we should leave the base and speak to the people. On the way from the building where we were with the Dutch soldiers and officers up to the gathered mass of population, it was about 250, 300 metres, and as we were leaving the base, there was some Serb soldiers who met us. Some of those Serb soldiers rushed over to the Dutch soldiers and disarmed them. And one of the Serb soldiers rushed to Mr. Nuhanovic and said: "Is that you?" And Ibro Nuhanovic stopped silent, I was also completely scared. I didn't -- we didn't answer. That Serb soldier then hit Mr. Nuhanovic. Mr. Nuhanovic went down on his knees, and then this Dutch sergeant who was escorting us tried to prevent that. And he said: No, no, that's not right. Let him go. After that, some 50 metres from there, we then set off towards General Mladic because we could see him about 50 metres from there. So then he said: Speak to the people. There were about 20.000 -- more than 20.000 people in front of us. They were waiting for this forcible deportation. We could foresee that the worst thing would happen, but we really couldn't speak about that to them, and we wouldn't be allowed to tell them what our foreboding was. General Mladic then asked the people gathered: Do you know these two men, pointing to me and Mr. Nuhanovic. People said yes, we do know them. They work at the school. One is a headmaster, one is a principal and the other one is a lecturer at the same school. What kind of people are they, he asked. And they said, normal people, ordinary people, honest people. And then General Mladic said don't create panic, you will all leave. First of all women with small children, elderly people, sick people, and the rest. But the departure and the way that we were forced to speak to this group of gathered people it was a specific type of psychological pressure which made us realise, as members of this so-called negotiating team, that we could do nothing. And the message to the population that was being deported is that they couldn't expect any help from the outside, not from international institutions, not from institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they should just accept that silently -- they should accept the situation, the situation whereby the male population was being separated from the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night of 12 July?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Inside the base with the interpreters and some officers of the DutchBat, except that we were not staying in the same room as the Dutch soldiers obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That night of the 12th, did you receive any information about what was going on outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: That same night, I left the building where the command of the Dutch battalion was seated. I had walked between 10 and 15 metres outside the building. You could hear screams, indiscernible voices, sounds of shooting. We couldn't tell how far this shooting was taking place. There was a lot of commotion, it was difficult to tell where the shots were coming from. But this made us realise, because we had seen Serb soldiers, that something horrible was going on there. The next morning, the next day, on the 13th of July, Camila Osmanovic entered into the base, and she had been with us the day before as part of the negotiating team. When she came, she confirmed what we had heard from other citizens, that outside the base in the night, between the 12th and the 13th of July, Serb soldiers had been killing people, massacring people. Some people had been massacred and their throats had been slit as they were on their way to fetch water for the people who were assembled there. She said that there had been separations near the elektroprivreda building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on 13 July, were you able to observe the continuing efforts to move the population out of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, also on the 13th of July, forcible deportation -- urgent deportation continued. I was shocked, as were the others, at the sheer speed of it, how quickly the deportation of Bosniaks from Potocari was unfolding. I could see the lorries and buses that were being used for the purpose, lorries with trailers from all over Bosnia and Herzegovina, or rather from all the various Serb-held areas. Our conclusion was that this was a planned operation, that it must have been planned well in advance because it was impossible to assemble 50 buses and 50 lorries in such short notice, within 24 hours only. It would have been impossible to have tens of thousands of people deported within just 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did much the same occur on the 13th as had occurred on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. And in the early afternoon hours on the 13th of July, the deportation of refugees outside the camp was completed, and the deportation of Bosniaks who were inside the base began. The same procedure of separating people was applied as with those who were outside the base. I remember inside the base, the areas where refugees could move were restricted. There were lines on the ground showing them the way on to the buses. And this lasted until about 2000 hours on the same day, this same procedure was applied. First women and children, and after them, the men. Who the men were, it was difficult to keep track at the time, but today we have thousands and thousands of exhumed bodies of Bosniak men from Srebrenica who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you know if the men that were staying in the DutchBat compound, the military-aged men, were allowed to be bussed out with the women and children?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Well, they were on their way at one point, but the Serb army were inside the camp on the 13th of July and outside the base, too. And they were the ones deciding who would be boarding the buses and who would be separated. But the great majority of men above 15 years of age were separated, put on to the buses, and deported. I must point out that even children below 15 years of age were sometimes executed. You can double check this using the International Red Cross list. I knew parents whose children were primary-school age, and their children were in the base on the 11th, 12th, and 13th of July. On the 13th of July, their mothers took them away, children aged between 12 and 14 years of age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there some Muslims that were inside the base that were allowed to stay with you and not be transported on the 12th and 13th, but were transported later?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. A group of 26 Bosniaks remained, including six or seven interpreters, interpreters for the Dutch Battalion, two or three for the Medicines San Frontiers, members of their families, 26 Bosniaks remained there until the 21st of July. However, as of the 13th of July, we were subjected to pressure by the Serb soldiers. They were searching the base to see if there were any Bosniaks still left. They were asking us questions as to what we had been doing during the war, if we had taken part in any of the military operations. That's what they asked me. There were several dozens of wounded persons, civilians, who were still in the camp after the 13th of July. Later on, they were transferred, or rather deported, to Tuzla. As far as I know, that's what the Medicines San Frontiers tried to achieve. However, some of those were killed, and some were exchanged months later. They were kept at a Serb camp in Batkovic after the interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was it that a certain number of Muslim interpreters and others were allowed to stay behind and be evacuated with DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact reason. I suppose the command of the Dutch battalion spoke on their behalf and put in a word for them. They said they needed these people until the very end of their mandate in Srebrenica. But I must repeat, I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So between the 13th, when the transportation was finished, and the 21st when you and DutchBat actually left, where did you stay?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Inside the base, the same building where the officers and the soldiers were, the Dutch soldiers, the Dutch army. But we were not sharing the same rooms. We were not sleeping in the same rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to take you now to the 17th of July while you were still at the Dutch base. Can you tell us what happened on the 17th regarding some documents.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 17th of July, as on the previous days, a group of wounded Bosniaks was there. They were all severely wounded. The Dutch battalion had a medical team but they were not capable of seeing to their wounds because they didn't have sufficient equipment to operate, to carry out surgery. On the 17th of July, I also noticed Serb soldiers and officers entering the building at which the command of the Dutch battalion was stationed. I noticed the same Serb officers staying for hours after that, and then I was called to come and see the deputy commander of the Dutch battalion. I went there to see the deputy commander. I met him there, and also met my former friend and colleague Miroslav Deronjic there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify who the deputy commander of the battalion is again?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Major Franken. I'm not sure my pronunciation is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know Mr. Deronjic who you just described?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: We worked together between 1990 and 1992, the Srebrenica secondary school. I saw Mr. Deronjic also at the meeting on the 12th of July at the Fontana Hotel in Bratunac. And I knew that since 1990, in addition to working as a teacher, he also held political office. He was the president of the Serbian democratic party during the war and you can say the war plunged him into politics and into politics of separation I was afraid of this -- of meeting again with Deronjic. I was afraid of facing him. So as I said, on the 17th of July, I was called by the command to meet Major Franken and my former colleague, Mr. Deronjic. Without long introductions, a proposal for an agreement was tabled for me to look at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was this about? What did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Learned about what, what exactly are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to them showing you an agreement, did anyone talk about it to you, Mr. Deronjic, or the Dutch?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay so --

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: This draft document was already prepared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So were you able to read it?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to read through it. It wouldn't have taken more than two or three minutes to read through. But I must say that I was surprised that this document was only presented after the Serb officers had arrived at the command and after they met with the Dutch officers. Two hours later, I was called to come over. I came. Deronjic brought this document. He put it on the table in front of me and told me to read through it and sign it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you read it?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I read the document. I noticed a number of shortcomings, the document began with a statement stating that it was the Bosniak civilian authorities, the Bosniak side, requesting the meeting, as I said at the beginning of my testimony today, myself, my colleague Camila, and Ibro were no formal or official representatives or even authorised representatives of the civilian bodies. There was the other remark at the beginning of that document, we were not the ones who actually requested the meeting. We were forced to attend. On the footage, you can see some details of the meeting. We were not even allowed to say what exactly we thought was necessary to ensure our survival.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the document, then. And you will hopefully see a side-by-side on the screen of the B/C/S version which is on the right and the English version which is on the left. And this is Exhibit 36.1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could look at the English version first, Mr. Mandzic, to tell me whether or not that is a photocopy of your signature on the left side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: My signature, if you look at the English version. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And if you could look at the second page of the B/C/S version, is that also your signature?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well then let's go down this document briefly and get your comments on it.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I assume this statement was put together by Mr. Deronjic even before he arrived in the base. Furthermore, declaration of representatives of the civilian authorities of the enclave of Srebrenica, I must point out that we were no formal representatives of the civilian authorities, nor did anyone authorise us to act on anyone else's behalf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would also mark as Exhibit P36.2 another English translation of this. This is a more complete and accurate translation of the B/C/S document. The field translation document had some names and some issues left out of it which I will ask Mr. Mandzic about briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, in the -- in paragraph 2 of Exhibit 36.2A, which is the English translation that we had done in The Hague, it says that "At our request, negotiations were conducted between representatives of our civilian authorities." Would you comment on whether or not you believe on the 11th and 12th, those were negotiations?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: In the second paragraph of this statement, it reads: "Our request." We never requested these negotiations. As I said at the beginning of my testimony, this was imposed on us by the Serb side. They asked the command of the Dutch battalion that Bosniaks attend these negotiations. So the second passage of this statement is simply false. Further, in the third passage, there is another mistake and another proof that Mr. Deronjic put this statement together by himself, without consulting anyone. Here we find Mrs. Camila's last name stated, her last name is Osmanovic, not Purkovic. Purkovic was actually her maiden name. And this is yet more proof that Mr. Deronjic took part in putting together this statement because Mr. Deronjic and Camila when she was still called Purkovic were schoolmates in secondary school, and he remembered her name as being Purkovic but now her last name was Osmanovic ever since she got married. Further --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was she there on the 17th to take part in this?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: She was inside the base on the 17th of July. But on account of the dramatic events unfolding between the 12th and the 13th of July, in her statement, she said she had heard screams, sounds of shooting, men being taken away, and she suffered a breakdown. She tried to commit suicide by hanging herself. Her brother got her off the rope. And from that point on, until the 21st, our evacuation, she was under constant surveillance by the medical team and her brother, who was also inside the base. But certainly, she should have been included in this list as a member of the negotiating team as well as Ibro Nuhanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did negotiations actually occur on the 12th and the 11th? Were you able to negotiate anything with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I don't think it would be proper to call those negotiations. Those were no negotiations of two equal sides, negotiating on equal terms in order to reach some kind of compromise. These were imposed negotiations, negotiations with an ultimatum. Our presence there was only required to put up a front for the international public, to have an appearance of trying to work together with representatives of the civilian authorities. But those who really decided the fate of the civilian population, or rather as Mr. Mladic, General Mladic said himself, whether the civilian population would vanish or not, it was really him. So please, you must understand that the term "negotiation" simply does not apply in this case. If you say negotiations, it makes the criminals appear in a much more favourable light. It's an insult to the victims and those who managed to survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Midway down the page, it talks about what the two sides agreed to. It says: "At the end of the negotiations between the two sides, the following was agreed..." If you could take a look at that and then comment on each of the sentences below that, and I'll read them to you. "That our civilian population could stay in the enclave or move out, depending on the wish of each individual." Was that a true statement? Does that reflect the wishes of the Muslim population at that time in your view?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: This is not true. None of the Bosniak representatives were there when this statement was being put together. The wording is by Mr. Deronjic, but the actual words were probably spoken by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at the next sentence. "Should we wish to move out from the enclave, it was agreed that we could choose where we wanted to go. We decided the entire civilian population move out of the enclave and be evacuated to the territory of Kladanj Municipality." Did the civilian population voluntarily decide to leave the enclave in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: In the period between the 6th of July, 1992, and the 13th of July, 1995, was subjected to a military coup by the Serb forces. So being forced to flee as refugees, their houses being torched, the killing and wounding of elderly people, even children. The situation after the 13th of July when forced deportations began, had there been international forces present and willing at that time to stop the Serb forces and force them to return to their initial positions, I can guarantee that all those people, the refugees, would return to their homes, even those that had been torched. Those people knew full well what deportations meant, that they would be uprooted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next paragraph says, "It was arranged that the evacuation would be carried out by the army and police of Republika Srpska and that UNPROFOR would supervise and provide an escort for the evacuation." Do you know if UNPROFOR was able to escort the evacuation or transportation of these people?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: This does not correspond what I can read here with the original agreement. On the first evening, the meetings between the 11th and 12th of July, Colonel Karremans was referring to the possibility of safe transport being organised for the refugees by UNPROFOR. But he said he wasn't sure if he could get the vehicles necessary for an evacuation on that scale. On the other hand, Mladic never asked any questions. He began deportations. And I remember one busload of Bosniaks arrived, the zone of delineation near Kladanj on the first day of deportations, about 40 persons who survived a massacre. Yet thousands and thousands of men were executed. And they were in Potocari in July of 1995, which does not correspond with this statement that I see here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the -- and the next statement says that the evacuations was carried out by the Serb side correctly and that this agreement had been -- the clauses of the agreement had been adhered to. So I take it you would agree with that also?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I disagree absolutely. It was a complete impossibility as far as we were concerned to influence the course of the deportation, rather to prevent it, myself and Mr. Nuhanovic. On the second and third day of the deportation, we asked Major Franken, deputy commander of the DutchBat, say we really have to stop this. And then they said that the Serbs were dictating the conditions and that there was nothing they could do about it to prevent this. This was a plan. We were able to see this in the field. The plan was to completely cleanse the enclave, to commit murder, mostly of adult male population with the intention to completely extinguish any trace of the fact that Bosniaks, Muslims lived in that area for centuries beforehand. And there was never a dilemma as to whether they would ever come back to their homes, to where they had lived before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This last paragraph says that "During the evacuation, there were no incidents on either side, and the Serb side has adhered to all the regulations of the Geneva Conventions and the international war law," which I grant by your previous answers you would disagree with. But what I want to ask you about now is in Exhibit 36.1, we see, as well as in the B/C/S version, handwritten in there "as far as convoys actually escorted by the UN forces are concerned." Can you tell us how that handwritten section got in there, who did it, and what the circumstances around it are?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I read these documents then, on the 17th of July. For a few moments, for a few minutes, I was speechless. I was by myself. Mr. Nuhanovic was separated. There was nothing known about him. Camila was completely psychologically drained, exhausted, and then the escort of Dutch soldiers and officers, they were looking at the deportation. I turned towards Major Franken. I looked him in the eye. I cannot describe to you, I cannot describe to you the look. I asked in his gaze for assistance, help. I asked for this statement to be denied, this Serb statement that had been put together. Major Franken understood this cry for help. He understood it speechlessly. We were communicating through looks because in front of Serb officers and Deronjic, he said "What do you think if we should add this addition?" Yes, but as far as convoys actually escorted by UN forces, because they only escorted the deported buses for a few hours up to Kladanj. And after that, Serbs had taken away all the vehicles, so the Dutch, as Major Franken said, were no longer able to continue with the escorts. So what he wanted is to make this statement relevant only for the buses that they had actually escorted. And that's how it was. So I said, okay, let's put this. Let's add this. As far as the addition is concerned, I didn't add it. This is not my handwriting. I think it was an interpreter who did it who was present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you sign these documents if the guts of them were not true?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: You must understand regarding the fate of thousands of people, men who were separated in the period between the 11th and the 13th of July, we had no idea what happened, whether they were executed or whether they had crossed on to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As far as the destiny of dozens, of hundreds of wounded civilians and others, we had no clue. We did not know whether they were executed, whether they had come to the territory under the control of BH. We believed they were under the control of the Serb army, and that was so. Further on, we had no assistance, we had no help by -- given by international institutions as a kind of protection. I mean the medical institutions, the Red Cross institutions. We had no contact with the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the other hand, we had Dutch soldiers, we had DutchBat, and I frequently tend to believe that they were more than scared. They couldn't wait to get rid of Srebrenica and the enclave and the life in the enclave, which was similar to life under medieval circumstances. And in addition to that at the base, there were 26 Bosniaks, 10 to 15 young men, interpreters with the UNPROFOR, with the MSF, young children, elderly people. All that was a condition for them to leave. We presumed that that was a condition for them to leave, so that some wounded would stay alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandzic. I don't have any further questions, Mr. President. I apologise. Our original estimate was a little long. I have certain advantage over my colleagues from the Krstic trial, and so I was able to get perhaps more to the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, since we just had a break for 40 days, and today is Monday, and the witness and some of the members of the Prosecution and the Defence team just arrived yesterday, I think we'll have an early break today and leave the cross-examination until tomorrow afternoon. Witness, I have to warn you, as I did with other witnesses, during your stay in The Hague, you are still under the oath. So do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do understand, Your Honours. I know the rules, and I accept the rules and respect them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I'm looking forward to seeing you tomorrow afternoon. Madam usher, would you please show the witness out of the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any matters to bring to the attention of the Trial Chamber? Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours. I just wanted to ask the Court's indulgence on a couple of matters. I have not filed a formal request for an extension of time to respond to a couple of the Prosecution's motions. But at this time, I'd like to ask the Court's indulgence and approval. We have -- I'd like to write a formal response to the request for judicial notice of adjudicated facts. I think the motion might have been filed June 23rd. So we're at the time limitation, if I could just ask the Court to extend the time until Monday, I would have that filed immediately. That's one, if there are no objections from the Prosecution. I haven't discussed it with Mr. McCloskey. The second one would be the Prosecution has filed a motion for clarification about the decision of the Trial Chamber from May 22nd. And I would ask the Court not to rule on the admissibility of the statements of the accused until the end of the Defence case because there's a lot of witnesses to be placed on the witness stand, cross-examinations of Prosecution witnesses and Defence witnesses that will be dealing with this issue. And I believe that under Rule 95 and 89, we have a lot of issues to deal with. But if the Court would allow me, I will respond to the Prosecution's motions just illuminating the legal issues that we will be dealing with and presenting during our consideration of the statements of the accused. So I'm asking the Court to not rule on the admissibility of the statements of the accused until all the evidence is heard, asking for an extension of time to respond to two Prosecution motions, the motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts and the motion for clarification by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have no problem with the brief extensions Ms. Sinatra has asked for to respond to our filings. I would object, however, to the putting off of the decision regarding the -- Mr. Jokic's statement until what must amount to months down the road. This is a significant issue. It's an issue that is traditionally in common law brought up prior to trial on a motion by the Defence to have the statement excluded, which was never done in this case. As Ms. De la Torre pointed out, I don't see why Defence witnesses would have any relevant significance to this issue nor has Ms. Sinatra stated any. So I don't see why an important issue such as this should be put off. Aside from giving each side a chance to make arguments on the various legal issues, this is an issue that's ripe and is ready for your decision once the arguments are done as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as for the first matter concerning the judicial notice, I think, you know, Ms. Sinatra's request is granted. We'll extend the time for you to reply on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As for that clarification of the admission of the statements of Mr. Jokic, we believe that Ms. Sinatra has a right to file a response on that matter. As for whether we have to postpone it until end of this case or not, I hope Ms. Sinatra could file written submissions listing your reasons for that so that we can consider the overall picture. Is that agreeable to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will be filing the reasons for our request. And I appreciate this extension of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we'll resume tomorrow afternoon at 2.15 in the Courtroom III, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one more thing, I would like to provide the Trial Chamber with this document from the US Treasury Department. I don't know if it's necessary for me to ask for political asylum at this point. But according to the rules of this executive order, I am committing a felony by appearing in Court. I intend to continue to appear in Court, but I do hope that the Trial Chamber and our judicial body of the Tribunal will consider this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll see the contents of your filings, to see whether there is a risk as you described.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just already stood up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The proceeding is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
